shorts.title: The Asteroid Hits in 60 Seconds — Which Hideout Saves You? ☄️
shorts.script: The asteroid hits in sixty seconds. Pick your hideout. Curl up inside a giant hollow tree. Crouch behind a wall of Triceratops. Squeeze into a tiny mammal burrow. Climb the highest hill for a view. Hide inside a T. rex nest. Cling to a giant pterosaur and fly. Lie flat in the open ferns. Stand on the beach and watch it land. Real answer: number 3, because burrowing animals had extra protection from the impact's after-effects. Probably your best bet. Comment your number.

shorts.title: Snowball Earth May Have Frozen Over — How Deep Do You Go? 🧊
shorts.script: Imagine the ocean frozen over. Pick your depth. One: standing on endless ice, wind howling. Two: right under the ice, faint light leaking through. Three: ten metres down, freezing blue twilight. Four: fifty metres, the last light fades. Five: two hundred metres. Total black. Six: one kilometre. Crushing cold, no light. Seven: the seafloor, kilometres under the ice. Eight: beside a superheated vent. Real answer: number 2, because photosynthesis can work under ice up to 20 metres thick. Life may have found a foothold there. Comment your number.

shorts.title: One Ice Age Night: Level 1 to 8 Tent-Mate — Who Keeps You Warm? 🧊
shorts.script: Minus forty in the Ice Age. Choose your bunkmate. Level one. A tiny Arctic lemming. Level two. An Arctic hare with warm fur. Level three: an arctic fox, curled into its tail. Level four. One reindeer, if it stays put. Level five. A bison, shaggy and heavy. Level six: a woolly mammoth. Huge, warm, sleepy. Level seven: a woolly rhino. Grumpy and horned. Level eight: a cave lion. Warm, and hungry. Real answer: number 6, because the woolly mammoth was covered in long guard hairs over a shorter undercoat. Mind the rollover. Comment your number.

shorts.title: Stranded With a T. rex for One Night — Where Do You Sleep? 🦖
shorts.script: One night in T. rex country. Pick your bed. A hollow log beside the creek. Across the river, wind blowing from the predator. Forty metres up an ancient conifer. In a hollow between enormous tree roots. Behind a mossy boulder at the tree line. In the ferns, right next to a nest. Exposed on the open mud flat. Right under a T. rex's searching nose. Real answer: number 2, because T. rex had a heightened sense of smell. Our imagined refuge keeps your scent blowing away from it. Comment your number.

shorts.title: Asteroid Tsunami Heading for the Coast — Where Do You Run? 🌊
shorts.script: The asteroid just hit the sea. The wave is coming. Shelter inside a small coastal cave. Climb the tallest dune on the beach. Climb high into a swamp tree. Ride a giant sea turtle. Swim far out into the open sea. Run inland for the faraway hills. Sleep out on the wide tidal flats. Go toward the glowing impact cloud. Real answer: number 6, because waves exceeded 100 metres. High ground far inland probably offers a chance. Comment your number.

shorts.title: Ocean Life Before Fish — How Deep Would You Go? 🌊
shorts.script: Before fish, before shells. How deep do you go? One: warm shallows over slimy microbial mats. Two: waist-deep, quilted creatures on the sand. Three: ten metres, storm waves churning sand. Four: fifty metres, quiet and dim. Five: the lip of a deep slope. Six: two hundred metres down the cold slope. Seven: a deep, still meadow of feathery fronds. Eight: volcanic ash raining down to bury everything. Real answer: number 7, because Charnia probably lived in deep water, well below the wave base. That fits our dark frond meadow. Comment your number.

shorts.title: Asteroid Hits Tonight — Level 1 to 8 Hideout: Where Do You Hide? ☄️
shorts.script: The asteroid hits tonight. You get one hideout. Level one: inside a hollow log. Level two: a burrow in a muddy riverbank. Level three: a deep cave in the hills. Level four: the top of the tallest tree. Level five: crouched among fallen boulders. Level six: on an open beach. Level seven: a cliff top, facing the impact. Level eight: ground zero, the shallow Yucatán sea. Real answer: number 2, because crocodile relatives probably survived the impact thanks to life in water and burrowing. Dig in by the river. Comment your number.

shorts.title: One Night on Pangaea — Which Campsite Do You Pick? 🌙
shorts.script: One supercontinent. One night. Where do you stop? A damp fern gully near the sea. A dry river bed, far inland. Right in the middle of the dunes. The middle of a huge salt flat. Beneath an overhang of warm red sandstone. Dug into a burrow in the dunes. On top of a lone mesa, storm coming. The exact heart of the supercontinent. Real answer: number 1, because the interior was drier, with extreme temperatures. The coast probably gives you better odds. Comment your number.

shorts.title: Dinosaur Winter After the Asteroid — Which Home Gets You Through? ❄️
shorts.script: The sun is gone for months. Choose your home. Stay in a warm nest under ferns. Take shelter inside a fallen log. Hide in a shallow sea reef. Sink into a quiet freshwater pond. Shelter in a narrow rock crevice. Drift far offshore in the open sea. Climb above the ash cloud. Stay exposed on open ground, through the cold. Real answer: number 4, because freshwater animals probably had low extinction rates after the impact. That record inspired our pond choice. Comment your number.

shorts.title: The Cambrian Ocean Has a Hunter — How Deep Do You Hide? 🦐
shorts.script: A spiked-claw hunter owns this ocean. Pick a depth. One: floating at the sunlit surface. Two: drifting in a plankton cloud. Three: hanging in open water, nowhere to hide. Four: beside a reef of cup-shaped sponges. Five: hovering just above a rippled sandbank. Six: lying flat on the seafloor mud. Seven: dropping down the dark reef cliff. Eight: suspended inside a bright sunbeam. Real answer: number 6, because this hunter probably avoided the sea bed, where grabbing prey risked claw damage. Lie flat. Comment your number.

shorts.title: Level 1 to 8 Ocean Armor in the Devonian — What Do You Wear? 🛡️
shorts.script: The Devonian sea at night. Choose your armor. Level one: a soft sponge. Cosy, useless. Level two: a shell with two neat halves. Level three: a spiky trilobite shield. Level four: a coiled ammonoid shell. Level five: a nautiloid cone, long as a spear. Level six: shark skin, without heavy armor. Level seven: solid bone plates across the head. Level eight: just bubbles. No armor at all. Real answer: number 7, because this fish wore bony armor plates across its skull and front half. Probably your toughest coat. Comment your number.

shorts.title: One Ice Age Night — Which Cave Do You Sleep In? 🧊
shorts.script: Ice Age Europe, a freezing night. Choose your shelter. A hollow dug into a snow drift. A shallow overhang, open to the valley. Under the roots of a fallen spruce. Under the ribs of an old mammoth. Right on the frozen lake shore. Deep in a cave littered with bones. A cave with fresh claw marks. The back of a cave bear's den. Real answer: number 2, because cave bears frequently hibernated in caves through winter. The open overhang is probably safer. Comment your number.

shorts.title: Pangaea's Supervolcano Wakes Up — Which Plan Saves You? 🌋
shorts.script: Pangaea's biggest volcano just woke up. Choose fast. Hide deep in a dense leafy thicket. Shelter in a cool river cave. Wallow in the swamp mud. Follow the predator with huge canine teeth. Dig in with the herd of tusked grazers. Climb a ridge to watch the eruption. Wade out into a warm sea bay. Walk straight onto the lava fields. Real answer: number 5, because this animal survived the extinction and thrived afterward. Fossils guide our imaginary choice. Comment your number.

shorts.title: Ocean of Giant Shelled Hunters — How Deep Do You Dare Go? 🐚
shorts.script: Two-metre shells with tentacles. How deep do you go? One: bathtub-warm tropical shallows. Two: a garden of early corals. Three: among drifting long cone shells. Four: the shelf edge, light fading. Five: below the shelf, dim and cool. Six: down the slope into the dark. Seven: the cold black basin floor. Eight: the airless black bottom water. Real answer: number 5, because Cameroceras thrived in shallow tropical seas. Just below the shelf is probably your best bet. Comment your number.

shorts.title: Giant Bug Tent-Mate, Level 1 to 8 — Who Shares Your Swamp? 🪲
shorts.script: One humid night in the coal forest. Pick a bunkmate. Level one: a springtail. Barely there. Level two: an early cockroach, very at home. Level three: a harvestman, all legs. Level four: a huge millipede. Calm and quiet. Level five: a giant mayfly at the opening. Level six: Meganeura, a dragonfly wide as a hawk. Level seven: a giant scorpion under the moss. Level eight: a swamp predator, mouth first. Real answer: number 4, because reported woody gut contents suggest Arthropleura may have eaten plants. Its diet is still uncertain. Comment your number.

shorts.title: Stranded on a Dinosaur Island — Where Do You Spend the Night? 🏝️
shorts.script: Jurassic islands, a warm lagoon. Pick your bed. Soft sand, just above the tide. Under the scrubby conifers on the ridge. Out on the warm lagoon flats. Inside a pterosaur roost on the rocks. Drifting on a big driftwood log. Dead centre of the dried lagoon mud. Wading out to the sponge reef. Swimming to the next island at night. Real answer: number 2, because the drying lagoons left sticky mud that trapped insects and small dinosaurs. Stay on firm ground. Comment your number.

shorts.title: Pangaea Is Overheating — Which Escape Plan Keeps You Alive? 🔥
shorts.script: Pangaea's tropics are too hot to live in. Rest on a shady tropical riverbank. Float in a warm equator lagoon. Dig into a hollow between dunes. Hide in a cave in red cliffs. Chase the giant monsoon storms. Settle by a volcanic hot spring. Trek thousands of kilometres south. Cross the inland desert at noon. Real answer: number 7, because extreme heat may have left Pangaea's tropics empty of land vertebrates. Your best bet is far south. Comment your number.
